*A note on notation before we start: the earliest files in this project use $t$ for the offset from the critical line and $y$ for the height — the reverse of the convention I've used ever since and will use for the rest of this series. I've translated the original 2023 notes into the later convention below: $t$ is the height, $u$ is the offset, $s = \tfrac12 + u + it$.*

## The question

Take a partial sum of the alternating zeta series, $f_N(s) = \sum_{n=1}^N (-1)^{n+1} n^{-s}$, and look at its squared modulus, $|f_N(s)|^2$. Multiply the sum out against itself — every term against every other term — and you get a double sum, a *Cauchy product*, with one entry for every pair of indices. Group those entries by which term of the original series they came from, and you get something with a very specific structure: a **grid**, indexed by $(l, n)$ with $1 \le l \le n$, where each cell corresponds to the product $l \cdot (n-l+1)$.

The question I was chasing in late 2023 was simple to state and hard to answer: can this grid tell you, on its own — before you know anything about actual zeros — that $|f_N(s)|^2$ is always at least as large as it would be with $u=0$, i.e. right at the critical line? If that's true for every $N$, in the limit, you've got real leverage on where zeros can live.

## Rays in a grid

Here's the structural fact that makes the grid tractable. Every pair $(l, n-l+1)$ has a greatest common divisor — call it $m$ — and once you divide it out, $l = m f_1$ and $n - l + 1 = m f_2$ for some coprime pair $(f_1, f_2)$. So instead of thinking of the grid as $N^2/2$ independent cells, think of it as a bundle of **rays**: one ray for every coprime pair $(f_1, f_2)$, and along each ray, $m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ walks outward.

The reason this matters: the oscillatory phase attached to cell $(l, n-l+1)$ is $\theta = -\tfrac{t}{2}\log\!\big(l/(n-l+1)\big) = -\tfrac{t}{2}\log(f_1/f_2)$ — and that depends only on the *direction* of the ray, $f_1/f_2$, not on how far out along it you are. Walk from $m$ to $m+1$ along a fixed ray and the phase doesn't move at all. Only the magnitude changes, growing like $(m^2 f_1 f_2)^{-(\text{something})}$.

## A parity coincidence

The original series carries a sign, $(-1)^{n+1}$, and that sign has to land somewhere once everything gets folded into cosines and sines. It turns out to land on parity: whether $m$ is odd or even at a given point on a ray determines — cleanly, mechanically, via whether $f_1, f_2$ are themselves odd or even — whether that cell's contribution comes in as a $\cos^2\theta$ term or a $\sin^2\theta$ term. Walk one more step along the ray, from $m$ to $m+1$, and the label *flips*.

So a ray doesn't alternate between two different phases — it alternates between two different **labels on the same fixed phase**, one step at a time: $\cos^2\theta$ at $m$, $\sin^2\theta$ at $m+1$, $\cos^2\theta$ at $m+2$, and so on.

## The convexity payoff

This is where it turns into an actual argument rather than bookkeeping. Since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, a consecutive pair of points on a ray — one labeled $\cos^2\theta$, the other $\sin^2\theta$ — is *literally* a convex combination of two values of the function

$$
f(x) = \tfrac12\left(x^{-(1/2-u)} + x^{-(1/2+u)}\right),
$$

evaluated at $x = m^2 f_1 f_2$ and $x = (m+1)^2 f_1 f_2$. And $f$ is convex on $(0,\infty)$ for any real $u$ — three lines of calculus confirm $f''(x) > 0$. Jensen's inequality then says the weighted combination you actually have is bounded below by $f$ evaluated at the weighted average of the two $x$-values. Do this for both the $\cos^2\theta$-first and $\sin^2\theta$-first pairings on the same pair of points, average the two resulting bounds, and apply Jensen a second time: everything collapses to a clean lower bound of the form $\big(\text{a weighted average of } m^2 \text{ and } (m+1)^2\big)^{-1/2}$ — exactly the value you'd get by setting $u = 0$ from the start.

## Why "the moon"

I called this the *moon* scenario, because of the shape of what's pairing up: two complementary crescents — the $\cos^2\theta$ share of one point, the $\sin^2\theta$ share of the next — that only complete each other, into a full convex combination, when you look at both halves together. Neither half alone is the whole picture; you need the linked pair.

## Where it actually leads

Chained all the way through the grid, this gives a real, general fact: certain sums built from $|f_N(s)|^2$ are bounded below by the value they'd take at $u=0$, via nothing but Jensen's inequality applied ray by ray. That's a genuine result, not a numerical observation — and it was the first real technique of this project, eight months before the spiral picture in [Chapter 2](../spiral-toward-a-center/index.qmd) gave the same underlying question a very different geometric face.

What it isn't is a proof that the bound is ever *strict* — that the inequality can't secretly be an equality at some $u \ne 0$. My own notes from that week end without answering that, mid-equation, on an unfinished attempt to compare $C(t,y,N)$ against $M(t,y,N)$ term by term. I'm leaving that exactly as honest as it actually was: a real piece of leverage, and an open door I didn't walk through before moving on to the next idea.
